\chapter{Country, City, Neighbourhood}
\label{ch:pais-y-lugar}
\hlchaptermodality{325}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five nested places in Spanish — el pais, la ciudad, el barrio, la plaza and el lugar — and say which one of them is Arabic rather than Latin.}

Complete ES-C325-lugar: say where you are from with pais and ciudad, place yourself in a barrio and a plaza, and name a spot with lugar.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el país]{el país — the widest circle you can be from}

\label{lesson:ES-C325-pais}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{more or less}, then \emph{not even}. (\emph{Más o menos}; \emph{ni siquiera}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item soy de… — the sentence this word finishes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-ÍS}, two beats, not one. The written accent on the \emph{í} is doing real work: without it, \emph{ai} would glide together into a single sound. The accent prises the two vowels apart and puts the weight on the second. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el país} — \textquotedblleft{}the country,\textquotedblright{} meaning a nation.

Latin \textbf{pāgus} was a country district — a stretch of land with a village in it, far from any city. Somebody who lived there was a \textbf{pāgānus}. Late Latin built \textbf{pāgēnsis}, \emph{belonging to the district}, and that word travelled north into French as \emph{pays} and came back over the mountains into Spanish as \textbf{país}.

English took \emph{pāgānus} twice, by two different roads, and never noticed. Through Church Latin it arrived as \textbf{pagan}: when the cities had changed religion the country districts had not, so \emph{country-dweller} and \emph{unconverted} became the same word. Through French \emph{paisant} — from that same \emph{pays} — it arrived as \textbf{peasant}. A pagan and a peasant are one Latin word wearing two English coats.

Spanish keeps the \emph{pays} family alive: \textbf{el paisaje} is the landscape, and \textbf{el paisano} is a fellow countryman.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five circles, from a whole country down to a single spot.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el país}
  \item \emph{mi país}
  \item \emph{soy de otro país}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{pāgus}? (A country district.) And which two English words both come from the person who lived in one? (\emph{Pagan} and \emph{peasant}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la ciudad]{la ciudad — a place named after the people in it}

\label{lesson:ES-C325-ciudad}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{not even}, then \emph{my country}. (\emph{Ni siquiera}; \emph{mi país}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item -dad — the ending, met once already with \emph{la verdad}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{syu-DAD}, the weight on the last beat. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft — an \emph{s} in Latin America, a \emph{th} in most of Spain — and \emph{ciu} runs through as one glide rather than three separate vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la ciudad} — \textquotedblleft{}the city.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had two ideas and kept them separate. \textbf{Urbs} was the buildings: walls, streets, stone. \textbf{Cīvitās} was the people: the body of \textbf{cīvēs}, citizens, who belonged to each other. Spanish let \emph{urbs} go except in bookish words like \emph{urbano}, and built its everyday word on the people instead. \textbf{Cīvitātem}, worn down through \emph{cibdad}, gives \textbf{ciudad}.

That is the second time you have watched Latin \emph{-tātem} land as Spanish \textbf{-dad}. \emph{Vēritātem} gave \emph{verdad}; \emph{cīvitātem} gives \emph{ciudad}. English took the same ending as \textbf{-ty}, so \emph{verity} and \emph{city} are the exact same road, walked twice.

The root is loud in English. A \textbf{citizen} is a \emph{cīvis}. \textbf{Civic} duty, \textbf{civil} war, a \textbf{civilian} rather than a soldier, and \textbf{civilization} itself are all the people-word rather than the building-word. Rome decided a city was who lived there, and both languages have carried that decision ever since.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The circle inside the country, and a Latin ending you can now spot on sight.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la ciudad}
  \item \emph{una ciudad grande}
  \item \emph{la ciudad y el país}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did Latin name the city after its walls or after its people? (Its people — \emph{cīvēs}.) And which English ending answers to Spanish \emph{-dad}? (\emph{-ty}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el barrio]{el barrio — an Arabic word for the part of town past the wall}

\label{lesson:ES-C325-barrio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the country}, then \emph{the city}. (\emph{El país}; \emph{la ciudad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hasta, azul and café — three words Spanish took from Arabic, already yours.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BA-rryo}, the weight on the first beat. The double \emph{rr} is a rolled trill, held long enough to buzz; \emph{io} at the end runs through as one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el barrio} — \textquotedblleft{}the neighbourhood,\textquotedblright{} the quarter of a town you live in.

This one is not Latin. Arabic \textbf{barr} was the open land — dry ground, the country outside. Andalusi Arabic made \textbf{barrī}, \emph{of the outside}, and in the walled towns of al-Andalus a \emph{barrī} was the district that had spilled past the wall and kept growing. Spanish took the word and lost the wall, so a \emph{barrio} became any quarter of any town.

You already carry three Arabic words in Spanish without having marked them as a set: \textbf{hasta}, from \emph{ḥattā}; \textbf{azul}, from \emph{lāzaward}, the blue stone; and \textbf{café}, from \emph{qahwah}. Nearly eight centuries of al-Andalus left something over a thousand words in Spanish, and they cluster where daily life is — buildings, water, farming, trade.

English then borrowed \emph{barrio} back out of Spanish without translating it, the way it took \emph{plaza} and \emph{patio}. The word has now crossed three languages and is still the same four sounds it started as.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The circle inside the city — and a reminder that Spanish is not only Latin.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el barrio}
  \item \emph{mi barrio}
  \item \emph{un barrio de la ciudad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Arabic \emph{barr} mean? (The open land outside.) And which three Arabic words in Spanish do you already say? (\emph{Hasta}, \emph{azul}, \emph{café}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la plaza]{la plaza — a word that means broad, and went everywhere}

\label{lesson:ES-C325-plaza}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the city}, then \emph{my neighbourhood}. (\emph{La ciudad}; \emph{mi barrio}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la calle — the street that runs into it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PLA-sa}, the weight on the first beat. The \emph{pl} stays a clean cluster with no vowel pushed in between, and the \emph{z} is an \emph{s} across Latin America and a \emph{th} in most of Spain. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la plaza} — \textquotedblleft{}the square,\textquotedblright{} the open space a town gathers in.

Greek \textbf{platýs} meant \emph{broad}. Greek speakers called a wide street a \textbf{plateîa hodós}, a \emph{broad way}, and dropped the \emph{way} until only \emph{plateîa} was left. Latin borrowed it as \textbf{platea}, and every Romance language then wore it down its own way: Spanish to \textbf{plaza}, Italian to \emph{piazza}, French to \emph{place} — and English took \emph{place} from French and \emph{plaza} from Spanish, so it is holding the same word twice without noticing.

\emph{Platýs} is broad in English too, once you hear it. A \textbf{plate} is a flat broad dish. A \textbf{plateau} is broad flat ground. A \textbf{platitude} is a flattened remark. And a \textbf{platypus} is \emph{platýs} plus \emph{poús}, foot — the broad-footed animal.

There is a thing worth marking about the Spanish town. The \emph{plaza} is not decoration; it is the centre a \emph{barrio} is arranged around, with the church on one side and the market on another. English-speaking towns tend to grow along a main street; Spanish-speaking ones grow around a middle, and \textbf{la plaza del pueblo} is where everybody ends up in the evening.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The middle of the neighbourhood, and a Greek word that reached English twice.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la plaza}
  \item \emph{la plaza del pueblo}
  \item \emph{la plaza del barrio}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Greek \emph{platýs} mean? (Broad.) And which English word is the same Latin \emph{platea} arriving through French? (\emph{Place}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el lugar]{el lugar — the same Latin word as luego, gone the other way}

\label{lesson:ES-C325-lugar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{my neighbourhood}, then \emph{the town square}. (\emph{Mi barrio}; \emph{la plaza del pueblo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item luego — the same Latin root, already yours.
  \item en primer lugar — this noun, already inside a phrase you can say.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lu-GAR}, the weight on the second beat. The \emph{g} before \emph{a} is hard, and the final \emph{r} is a single flick of the tongue rather than a roll. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el lugar} — \textquotedblleft{}the place,\textquotedblright{} a spot rather than a town.

Latin \textbf{locus} was a place. Spanish took it twice and let the two copies drift apart until they stopped sounding related.

One copy stayed about space. \emph{Locālis}, \emph{belonging to a place}, wore through Old Spanish \emph{logar} into \textbf{lugar} — a spot, a position, somewhere something goes. The other copy turned into time. \emph{In locō}, \emph{in that place}, became \emph{luego}, and what began as \emph{there} slid into \emph{then} — which is why you have been saying \textbf{hasta luego} since almost the beginning without meeting the place inside it.

You have also been carrying the noun whole. \textbf{En primer lugar} — \emph{in the first place} — is this word, holding the same job it holds in English.

English kept \emph{locus} untranslated for a point in space, and built \textbf{local}, \textbf{locate}, \textbf{location}, \textbf{allocate} and \textbf{dislocate} on it. It also has the French version: \emph{lieu} is \emph{locus} worn down, so a \textbf{lieutenant} is a \emph{place-holder}, the officer who stands in somebody else's spot — and \emph{in lieu of} is \emph{in the place of}, still doing its Latin job in an English sentence.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five circles: country, city, neighbourhood, square, spot. You can now say where you are from and where you are.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el lugar}
  \item \emph{otro lugar}
  \item \emph{un lugar en el barrio}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which everyday farewell has \emph{locus} hiding inside it? (\emph{Hasta luego}.) And what does a \textbf{lieutenant} hold? (Somebody else's place.)
\end{tcolorbox}
